You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:

S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",

     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: $V_{out}$ between 1.8V and 3.6V, ripple $\le 0.05$V, startup $\le 0.4$s, settled $\le 0.02$V.
    *   Piezo Model: Sinusoidal current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ || $C_p$ || $20\text{M}\Omega$.
    *   Operating conditions: S1-S6 (vary $I_p$, $f$, $C_p$, $R_L$).
    *   Key constraints: Cold start from 0V, 0.8s simulation.

    *   `SSHI_FBR_Zener`:
        *   Topology: Full bridge rectifier (FBR) + an inductor $L$ and switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo (SSHI-like), plus a Zener clamp and a storage capacitor $C$.
        *   Results:
            *   $V_{avg}$ failed S2, S4, S5.
            *   $V_{max}$ passed.
            *   Ripple failed (too large).
            *   Startup failed (too slow).
            *   Settled failed (still drifting).
        *   Analysis: The SSHI inductor/switch is intended to flip the charge of $C_p$. However, the FBR adds significant diode drops (two diodes in series, $\approx 0.5\text{V}$ total). With $V_{oc} \approx 3.2\text{V}$, the available voltage is reduced. The drift and ripple issues suggest the storage capacitor $C$ is too small, but the startup is too slow, suggesting it's too large or the charging current is too low. Actually, the "settled" and "ripple" failures are typical when the capacitor is too small to smooth the rectified pulses or when the circuit hasn't reached equilibrium.

    *   `FBR_Zener`: Failed screening. Too much power loss through diodes for weak excitation (S4).

    *   The piezo voltage is low ($\approx 3.2\text{V}$ amplitude). Full-bridge Schottky rectifiers (FBR) lose $2 \times 0.25\text{V} = 0.5\text{V}$ per half cycle.
    *   Standard SSHI uses a switch to invert the voltage across $C_p$, effectively increasing the voltage seen by the rectifier.
    *   Wait, looking at `SSHI_FBR_Zener`: The inductor $L$ and switch $S$ are connected from `pzp` to `pzn` (via `n1`). This is a basic L-C inversion.
    *   The failure in `SSHI_FBR_Zener` for $V_{avg}$ on S2, S4, S5 means not enough power is delivered.
    *   The failure in `ripple` and `settled` means the output capacitor is either too small (ripple) or the charging rate is too slow (settled/startup).

    *   A standard half-bridge or a more efficient charge pump might work.
    *   Since the voltage is low, let's try a Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction (SECE) or a Parallel-SSHI (P-SSHI) topology.
    *   SECE typically uses a switch to connect the piezo to a storage capacitor at the peaks of the voltage.
    *   Let's try a simpler approach: a Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI) but with a more efficient rectification.
    *   Actually, the most efficient way to handle low voltage is often a synchronous rectifier or a charge pump. But we are limited to switches and diodes.
    *   Let's consider a "synchronous rectifier" using the SYNC switches. However, the SYNC switches only close for a short `ton`. They aren't meant for continuous conduction. They are meant for the $L-C$ resonance (inversion).

    *   The `SSHI_FBR_Zener` was:
        Piezo || (L1 + S1) || (D1...D4 bridge) -> C1.
        Wait, the FBR is in parallel with the L-S inversion circuit.
    *   If we use a half-bridge (one diode) instead of a full-bridge, we lose less voltage but only harvest half the cycles. But the inversion circuit (SSHI) helps.
    *   Actually, a common efficient topology is the "Synchronous Switch" where the L-S circuit flips the charge, and a single diode (or bridge) moves it to the storage capacitor.
    *   Let's try an SSHI with a simpler diode interface (half-wave) or a better arranged full-wave.
    *   Looking at the `SSHI_FBR_Zener` results, the ripple is very high. This is because the energy comes in pulses. A larger $C$ would fix ripple but slow down startup.
    *   Wait, if $V_{avg}$ is low on S2, S4, S5, we need more power.
    *   The current design `SSHI_FBR_Zener` had the FBR and the L-S in parallel.
    *   Let's try a different SSHI arrangement: The "Parallel-SSHI" (P-SSHI).
        P-SSHI: Piezo $C_p$ is in parallel with a capacitor $C_{buffer}$ (or just the storage $C_{out}$), and the switch $S$ and inductor $L$ are used to flip the charge.
        Actually, a simpler way is the SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction).
        SECE: Switch connects $C_p$ to $C_{out}$ only at the peaks.
        Wait, SECE requires a switch to transfer the charge.
        Let's try:
        1. Piezo terminals `pzp`, `pzn`.
        2. Switch `S1` connects `pzp` to `out` at the positive peak.
        3. Switch `S2` connects `pzn` to `out` at the negative peak? No, that would short `out` to ground if not careful.
        4. SECE usually uses an inductor.

    *   Let's try a "Synchronous Rectifier" approach using switches if possible, but the SYNC is limited to `ton`.
    *   What if we use a bridge with only 2 diodes and 2 switches?
        D1: `pzp` to `out`
        S1: `pzn` to `0` (closed at positive peak)
        D2: `pzn` to `out`
        S2: `pzp` to `0` (closed at negative peak)
        This is a synchronous bridge. But the `ton` is too short for this.

    *   Let's go back to the basics: SSHI with a bridge.
        The `SSHI_FBR_Zener` had $L$ and $S$ in parallel with the piezo. This flips the charge of $C_p$ *before* it's rectified.
        The issue was the FBR's diode drops.
        If we use a half-wave rectifier (one diode) and SSHI, we only lose one diode drop.
        Let's try:
        L-S flip circuit in parallel with piezo.
        Diode from `pzp` to `out`.
        Capacitor `out` to `0`.
        But this only harvests the positive half-cycle. SSHI flips the negative to positive, so it should work.

    *   Wait, the `S3` case (strong excitation, light load) had $V_{avg} = 3.41\text{V}$ and $V_{max} = 3.41\text{V}$ (Zener clamped). This means the SSHI+FBR is capable of producing enough voltage. The failure on S2, S4, S5 is due to the diode drops being too high relative to the harvested energy.

    *   Let's try a "Charge Pump" or "Voltage Doubler" if the voltage is too low. But the voltage isn't that low; it's the efficiency that's the problem.

    *   Actually, the most robust low-voltage harvester is the SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction).
        In SECE:
        - Inductor $L$ is in series with a switch $S$ and a diode $D$.
        - Switch $S$ connects `pzp` to $L$ at the voltage peak.
        - After $S$ opens, the energy in $L$ is transferred to $C_{out}$ through $D$.
        - This happens at both peaks.

    *   Let's refine the SECE:
        - $S_1$ connects `pzp` to `n1`.
        - $L_1$ connects `n1` to `n2`.
        - $D_1$ connects `n2` to `out`.
        - $S_2$ connects `pzn` to `n1`? No.
        - To do it for both peaks:
          - Path 1: $S_1$ (`pzp` to `n1`), $L_1$ (`n1` to `n2`), $D_1$ (`n2` to `out`).
          - Path 2: $S_2$ (`pzn` to `n3`), $L_2$ (`n3` to `n4`), $D_2$ (`n4` to `out`).
          - $S_1$ closes at positive peak (`edges: pos`).
          - $S_2$ closes at negative peak (`edges: neg`).

    *   Wait, that's a lot of components. Let's try a simpler SECE:
        - $S_1$ connects `pzp` to `n1` (`edges: both`).
        - $L_1$ connects `n1` to `n2`.
        - $D_1$ connects `n2` to `out`.
        - But this only works for one polarity. To handle both, we need a bridge.
        - If we put the SECE extraction ($S \to L \to D$) after a bridge? No, that's worse.
        - What if we use the $S \to L \to D$ structure and a bridge to ensure `out` always receives positive charge?
          - $S_1$ connects `pzp` to `n1` (`edges: both`).
          - $L_1$ connects `n1` to `n2`.
          - $D_{bridge}$ (full bridge) from `n2` to `out`. (Too many components).

    *   Let's try a simpler "SSHI" with a half-bridge and a Zener clamp.
        L1: `pzp` to `n1`
        S1: `n1` to `pzn` (ctrl G1, `edges: both`)
        D1: `pzp` to `out` (DSCH)
        C1: `out` to `0`
        DZ1: `out` to `0` (DZ33)
        This flips the charge of $C_p$ and then rectifies the positive peaks.
        Let's check if this is enough.
        With $L$ and $S$, the voltage across $C_p$ is flipped.
        Cycle:
        1. $V_{pzp}$ rises to $V_{peak}$.
        2. $S_1$ closes, $L$ and $C_p$ resonate, $V_{pzp}$ goes to $-V_{peak}$.
        3. $V_{pzp}$ rises again from $-V_{peak}$ towards $V_{peak}$.
        The diode $D_1$ conducts whenever $V_{pzp} > V_{out} + V_{drop}$.
        This is a half-wave rectifier but it's effectively full-wave because of the flipping.
        This uses: L1, S1, G1, D1, C1, DZ1 (6 components). Very efficient.

    *   Wait, the `SSHI_FBR_Zener` had the FBR (4 diodes). If we replace the FBR with a single diode, we reduce the voltage drop from $2 \times 0.25\text{V}$ to $1 \times 0.25\text{V}$. This might be the key for S2 and S4.

    *   `L1`: `pzp` to `n1`
    *   `S1`: `n1` to `pzn` (ctrl: `G1`)
    *   `G1`: `ton` $\approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$, `edges: both`, `phase: 0`.
    *   `D1`: `pzp` to `out` (DSCH)
    *   `C1`: `out` to `0`
    *   `DZ1`: `out` to `0` (DZ33)
    *   Wait, if the switch $S_1$ flips the voltage, the diode $D_1$ only takes the positive parts. Let's double-check.
        At $t=0$, $V_{pzp} = 0$. It rises to $V_{peak}$. $D_1$ conducts, $C_{out}$ charges.
        At $t=t_{peak}$, $S_1$ closes. $V_{pzp}$ flips to $-V_{peak}$. $D_1$ is off.
        $V_{pzp}$ then rises from $-V_{peak}$ back to $V_{peak}$. $D_1$ conducts again.
        This effectively doubles the frequency of charging pulses and reduces the voltage drop.

    *   Wait, will $V_{pzp}$ reach $V_{out} + 0.25\text{V}$?
        $V_{oc} = 3.2\text{V}$. With SSHI, the peak voltage is higher.
        Actually, the voltage across $C_p$ in SSHI can reach $2 \times V_{oc}$ in the ideal case.
        So $V_{pzp}$ can reach $\approx 6\text{V}$. The diode drop $0.25\text{V}$ is negligible.

    *   Now, let's address ripple and settling.
        Ripple $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$ is quite tight.
        $C_{out}$ must be large. But if $C_{out}$ is too large, `tup` (startup) will be too slow.
        `tup` $\le 0.4\text{s}$.
        Let's try $C_{out} = 10\text{uF}$ to $47\text{uF}$.
        The settled check (`dv` $\le 0.02\text{V}$) also requires the capacitor to be large enough to reach equilibrium or the simulation to be long enough.

    *   Wait, the `SSHI_FBR_Zener` had $C_1 = 10\text{uF}$ and failed ripple/settled.
        Let's try a larger $C_1$ for the half-bridge version.
        Since we have more voltage headroom (one diode instead of two), maybe we can afford a larger $C_1$.

    *   Let's try two designs:
